subject: Biology
title: Designer Babies: The Ethics Debate
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Designer Babies: The Ethics Debate.

hook.text: What if parents could choose their child's eye color, height, or intelligence before birth?

buildup.text: Preimplantation genetic testing already screens embryos for serious genetic diseases.

discovery.text: CRISPR could theoretically go further—editing traits like appearance or athletic ability.

twist.text: Most traits involve hundreds of genes. Designing a 'perfect' baby is far more complex than it sounds.

climax.text: The line between preventing disease and enhancing traits raises deep ethical questions.

quiz.question: Why is designing specific traits in babies extremely complex?
options: Most traits involve hundreds of genes
DNA cannot be edited at all
Traits are determined only by environment

details.summary: The term designer babies refers to using genetic technologies to select or modify traits in embryos beyond disease prevention. While currently limited, advancing gene-editing tools could eventually enable selection for intelligence, appearance, or athletic ability.
details.whyItMatters: Genetic enhancement of embryos raises questions about equity, consent, and what it means to be human. If only wealthy families access enhancements, genetic technology could deepen social inequality across generations.
takeaways: Genetic selection for disease prevention is already practiced in IVF clinics
Enhancement for non-medical traits raises significant ethical concerns
Most complex traits involve too many genes to engineer reliably today

faq.question: Can we currently create designer babies?
faq.answer: Not in any meaningful sense for complex traits. Pre-implantation genetic testing can screen embryos for single-gene disorders in IVF, but traits like intelligence involve thousands of genes and cannot be engineered with current technology.

faq.question: Why is germline editing more controversial than somatic editing?
faq.answer: Somatic edits affect only the treated individual. Germline edits change eggs, sperm, or embryos and are inherited by all future descendants. This means any mistakes or unintended effects would propagate through generations without the consent of those affected.
